items.body:
<!-- For information about contributing see: https://github.com/supercollider/supercollider/wiki/Contributing-directory -->
<!-- If you used AI for any part of the PR, please see https://github.com/supercollider/supercollider/blob/develop/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md#usage-of-ai-tools -->

## Purpose and Motivation

<!-- Please provide a description, even if you are linking to a related Issue or PR. -->
<!-- If this fixes an open issue, link to it by writing "Fixes #555." -->

This PR fixes several bugs/regressions with NRT synthesis in scsynth and supernova.

### Changes:

- scsynth: ignore `-S` (= sample rate) command line option if `-N` (= non-rt synthesis) has been provided. The `-N` option has a mandatory sample rate argument that we consider authoritative.

  Currently, NRT synthesis is completely broken on develop because `ServerOptions - asOptionsString` has been changed to pass *all* options (https://github.com/supercollider/supercollider/pull/7111), so when you pass a `ServerOptions` object to `Score -recordNRT`, it would accidentally override the `sampleRate` argument rate with the default sample rate (= 0) in the `ServerOptions`.

- supernova: fix broken sound input in NRT synthesis. Closes https://github.com/supercollider/supercollider/issues/7108.

  The problem was that the number of inputs was taken from `audio_backend::get_input_count()`, which always returns 0. (NRT synthesis does not open the "real" audio backend, so methods of `audio_backend` just report the initial values.) Instead, `run_scheduler_tick` must take the number of inputs and outputs from the `World` structure. This is a regression introduced by https://github.com/supercollider/supercollider/pull/4575/changes.
  
- supernova: make sure that the number of input busses matches the number of input soundfile channels. In case of a mismatch, bash the former to the latter and post a warning. This matches the behavior of scsynth.

- supernova: make sure that we actually process the very last block. This makes sure that the output file has the same size on both Servers.

- supernova: fix threaded soundfile reading. Previously, the behavior was completely indeterministic because the input thread would set an atomic flag on EOF. This caused the sound input to become silent at a seemingly random point. Now we keep track of the read position on the main thread, so we can reliably detect the EOF and output silence accordingly.

- supernova: add a dedicated implementation for `non_rt_functor::init_thread()` instead of forwarding to `rt_engine_functor::init_thread()`.

  The latter would attempt to set a realtime thread priority, which would in turn call Jack API functions on a `NULL` client. For some reason this only crashed on certain systems, in particular on the CI. This very likely fixes the problem with NRT synthesis discussed in https://github.com/supercollider/supercollider/pull/7567#issuecomment-6008257586.

- testsuite: add `TestNRTSynthesis` test.

  `test_nrtSynthesisInputWorks` reads one of the example files via `SoundIn.ar` and outputs it unchanged via `Out.ar`. We then check that
  - the output file has the correct sample rate and number of channels
  - the output file is not shorter than the input file
  - the size difference between the input and output file is not greater than the Server block size
  - any extra samples in the output file are properly set to zero.
  
  We do all of this with both Servers!

- scsynth: use `std::vector` as the backing buffer for `nextOSCPacket` and grow it on demand instead of (re)allocating a new buffer for every packet.

- supernova: read the input in larger chunks; sleep for 1 ms if the ringbuffer is empty, don't just spin and waste CPU cycles (= power)

- supernova: fix a bug in the `time_tag` class and add missing methods

- Various code cleanups

---

Once this PR is accepted, I want to rebase and squash everything into three commits:
1. the scsynth fixes
2. the supernova fixes
3. the unit test

<!-- For information about contributing see: https://github.com/supercollider/supercollider/wiki/Contributing-directory -->

## Motivation

There are multiple issues and PRs that tackle aspects of the interdependent issues of managing SC extensions with some kind of separation from the user install. This is for the purpose of:
1. managing/archiving full projects with a set of extensions and plugins independent from the system/user installation, 
2. creating "standalone" SC distributions that include such set of plugins and extensions and can be run as an independent app.

Note: a "Standalone" version of SuperCollider was an existing feature in the Cocoa days (before SC-IDE came along) and allowed creating macOS "apps" that were self-contained with all extensions included (i.e. could be sent to a performer for them to run the electronics themselves in rehearsal or performance). There used to be some workarounds to get a similar functionality with SC IDE, but I don't believe we ever had a fully fleshed-out solution.

Additionally, one of the issues below discusses a different set of extensions for the upcoming SC 3.15 due to updated server plugin API. I think that if we figure out a nice way to create separate environments, that would allow users to test SC 3.15 in the new "standalone" mode (however that would look).

## Existing discussions/PRs/approaches

- SuperCollider Projects https://github.com/supercollider/supercollider/issues/311
- New Standalone Approach https://github.com/supercollider/supercollider/pull/5898
- Linux AppImage Standalone https://github.com/supercollider/supercollider/pull/5938
- https://github.com/supercollider/supercollider/issues/4353
- https://github.com/supercollider/supercollider/issues/7699
- Change folder structure for SC 3.15 https://github.com/supercollider/supercollider/issues/7677
- IIRC @capital-G mentioned the planned package manager as a possible solution, as that could pack a version of sclang, scsynth, class library, extensions, and plugins into a single "package"

## Description of Proposed Feature

Here's my estimation of what needs to be addressed, in general:
- managing paths for sclang extensions
  - language config files only provides a partial functionality for this, since paths need to be absolute (the last time I checked).
  - we have a "standalone mode" for sclang, but that excludes ALL extensions, and the need absolute paths doesn't allow to simply pack this into a SuperCollider installation
- managing server plugin paths
  - these can be included through server command line, but I don't believe we have a mechanism of synchronizing this with sclang-config
  - I'm not sure if we can currently exclude paths in the servers?
- including/excluding Startup file from the user or bundled with the application
- creating an actual portable application (OS-dependent packaging)
  - we'd need to decide if this is something one needs to build themselves, or if there's a template a user can download and adapt 
    - the latter is of course more user friendly, but is it feasible?
  - macOS: the bundle is already self-contained, but there's a question whether user extensions would go inside (issues with code signing) or outside of it (issue with packaging/distribution)
  - Linux: there's some work done on AppImage; we also currently offer (non-portable) Flatpak, could that be used for standalone template?
  - Windows: the non-installer version is already a folder that can be placed anywhere and run in-place
 
## Plan for Implementation

Before I start _yet another thread_ on managing extensions, can we take a birds-eye view on this, particularly on the mechanism of specifying extension paths for sclang and the servers?

E.g. I'd start with reworking the sclang standalone mode (or add a new flag/parameter) so that it includes the bundled library, but excludes system extensions. Then we'd need to propagate this to the server(s). Once we have that functionality in the sclang/scsynth/IDE ecosystem, we could figure out how to bundle that into a standalone app... But maybe this is not the best approach. Let's discuss this...

items.body:
Just noticed this, somewhat related to the various path searching complications. At first I thought this might be another issue with my installation but after looking at the code I think it is a "bug" because server scans for plugins even in directories that are excluded for sclang. This may or may not be a linux only issue - would need to check on other machines.

## Environment

3.15. dev, ubuntu studio 24.04

## Steps to reproduce
Have some extension installed that includes server plugins, with path `/path/to/extension`. It will be more obvious if the plugin normally throws an error or warning, such as API incompatibilities with older plugins
In `sclang_config.yaml`, exclude that extension.

```yaml
excludePaths:
  - /path/to/extension
 # and to make perfectly sure, also set
excludeDefaultPaths: true 
```
start sclang, and then boot scsynth or supernova without having set a ` ugenPluginsPath`.


## Expected vs. actual behavior
Expected behavior: the plugins in `/path/to/extension` are _not_ scanned by the server
Actual behavior: they are, as the server complains about API incompatibilities.

```
ERROR: API version mismatch: /path/to/extension/and/within/that/path/to/plugin.scx
    This plugin uses an unknown version of the interface.
    You may need to update SuperCollider in order to use it.
    (Plugin's API version: 5. Expected: 6)
```
The issue here is NOT about the error, but rather that (ideally) that path shouldn't be scanned by scsynth at all, hence no error raised in connection with it. Would be nice in particular when working across the API change (i.e., I have old plugins installed and it would be cool to just disable them via sclang_config).

## Code that would have to be changed somehow (I think)
supercollider/server/supernova/server/main.cpp
supercollider/server/scsynth/SC_Lib_Cintf.cpp

items.title: Unifying server booting posting
items.body:
This is in the interest to discuss possible refinement to the server booting posting, continuing discussion in #7018 

The question is how to present the information about requested devices consistently.

#7018 focuses on the listing part of the process, in that PR posting looks about like this:

*macOS (coreaudio)*

```
*** Scsynth booting
2 Available Audio Devices:
- "MacBook Pro Microphone"   (1 ins, 0 outs)
- "MacBook Pro Speakers"   (0 ins, 2 outs)

Booting with:
  In: "MacBook Pro Microphone" (Streams: 1 , 0), 1 outs
  Out: "MacBook Pro Speakers" (Streams: 1 0), 2 ins)
  Sample rate: 44100.000000
  SC_AudioDriver's block size: 512
SuperCollider 3 server (scsynth) ready.
```

*Windows (portaudio)*

```
*** Scsynth booting
1 Available Audio Devices:
- "Windows WASAPI : Speakers(High Definition Audio Device)"   (0 ins, 2 outs)

Requested devices:
  In:
  - (default)
  Out:
  - (default)

Selecting default system output device
WARNING: no input device selected, input is disabled.

Booting with:
  Out: "Windows WASAPI : Speakers(High Definition Audio Device)" 2 out
  Sample rate: 48000.000
  Latency (in/out): 0.000 / 0.022 sec
  Sample rate: 48000.000000
  SC_AudioDriver's block size: 64
SuperCollider 3 server (scsynth) ready.
```

Portaudio backend informs explicitly about which devices were requested and whether default device was selected.

Coreaudio backend mentions streams.

I'd suggest to remove the streams info and to fold the information about requested/default devices into the "Booting with" section in both backends, so that we end up with something like:

*default*
```
Booting with:
  In: "MacBook Pro Microphone" (1 out) - default
  Out: "MacBook Pro Speakers" (2 ins) - default
```
*matching requested device*
```
Booting with:
  In: "MacBook Pro Microphone" (1 out) - as requested
  Out: "MacBook Pro Speakers" (2 ins) - as requested
```
*NOT matching requested device*
```
Booting with:
  In: "MacBook Pro Microphone" (1 out) - different than requested ("Some other device name")
  Out: "MacBook Pro Speakers" (2 ins) - different than requested ("Some other device name")
```

Maybe there's an option to streamline the wording of the last one? Maybe put `DIFFERENT` in all caps?

I'd like to discuss this before making a PR. Please share your thoughts/feedback!

items.body:
https://github.com/supercollider/supercollider/pull/7395 introduces SynthDef v3.

Most importantly, it adds a *size* (int32) field at the beginning of the synth definition so that it can be extended in the future without having to bump the version. The idea is that fields can be *added to the end* of the synth definition and parsers can simply check the remaining bytes to determine which of these new fields are present. New fields must be optional so that older parsers can just ignore them.

Since we are bumping the version from 2 to 3, this is our historic chance to make any further modifications to the SynthDef file structure :)

For example, here's another upcoming change: the reblock/resample PR (https://github.com/supercollider/supercollider/pull/7402) will add some new mandatory fields. 

The purpose of this issue is to collect ideas so that they are not forgotten:

- we could add the number of local soundbuffers as a field. This way we can actually allocate the SndBuf array as part of the Graph structure itself, like we do with all the other arrays. The `MaxLocalBufs` UGen is just a hack that wouldn't have been necessary if the old SynthDef format was extendable. We likely have to keep it for backwards compatibility, but with the new version it would simply do nothing.

- add the number of local audio and control busses + add members to `World` structure. This way the bus buffers can be allocated as part of the Graph structure. Also, the local busses would be accessible from plugins; currently they are completely private. This would allow to write your own local bus plugins, for example.

- add a list of symbols, similar to the list of constants. This would allow users to pass symbols as UGen inputs. (The UGen would interpret the input as an index into the symbol table. See https://github.com/supercollider/supercollider/issues/7403#issuecomment-4019902381 and the following posts.)

- ?

items.title: Plugin API Extension: Freeing & Copying Buffers
items.body:
<!-- For information about contributing see: https://github.com/supercollider/supercollider/wiki/Contributing-directory -->

## Motivation

Extending the plugin API to introduce 
1. a `fBufFree` that corresponds to existing `fBufAlloc` 
2. a way to copy `SndBuf` instances that works transparently between scsynth and supernova

## Description of Proposed Feature

The plugin API allows you to allocate new buffer data. This is useful if you are writing buffer processing facilities that work like `BufGen`s. For a `BufGen` all the housekeeping is taken care of by `BufGenCmd`. However this limits you to generators that only produce a single output buffer. If you need more, then you have to implement your own sequenced command similar to `BufGenCmd`, and to make this work you need to be able to free buffer data (stage 4) and copy `SndBuf` instances (stage 3): 

https://github.com/supercollider/supercollider/blob/eb2bc5d25a922a01f74412a84caed24eef4c186c/server/scsynth/SC_SequencedCommand.cpp#L347-L368

In FluCoMa, we have our own equivalent sequenced commands because some of our buffer processing needs more than one output buffer (e..g for decomposing sounds). We have cheated and simply been calling the boost aligned free function that scsynth uses. Copying the buffer instances is trivial in scsynth. 

However, not having API support for these two operations is one of the [blockers for us making FluCoMa work with supernova](https://github.com/flucoma/flucoma-sc/issues/90): we would need to be aware of two sets of implementation details to free buffers, rather than the ideal of zero. `SndBuf` in supernova is not copyable and it has its own internal function for copying them field by field. 

## Plan for Implementation

Implementation for scsynth is trivial, and road tested in FluCoMa for a few years now with no problems. 

e.g
```c++
void fBufferFree(void* data) { zfree(data); }
void fBufferCopy(SndBuf* dst, const SndBuf* src) { *dst = *src; } 
```

Supernova, I'm less certain, because I don't quite follow how the buffer memory is being managed, but the buffer copying is already implemented
```c++
void fBufferFree(void* data) { free_aligned(data); /* ? */}
void fBufferCopy(SndBuf* dst, const SndBuf* src) { sndbuf_copy(dst, src); } 
```

items.title: Safety clipper should also filter out NaNs and infinities
items.body:
<!-- Please see CONTRIBUTING.md for guidelines. -->

## Motivation

CoreAudio freaks out if it is asked to output a NaN or infinity, generally requiring the user to kill the coreaudio process and restart it. Either of the following will repro the issue:

```
{ DC.ar(0)/DC.ar(0) }.play
{ DC.ar(1)/DC.ar(0) }.play
```

## Description of Proposed Feature

If the safety clipper is enabled, it should replace NaNs and infinities with 0. Tying these features together seems reasonable, as it seems extremely unlikely to me that someone would want to enable the safety clipper but also allow NaNs and infinities to mess up CoreAudio.

## Plan for Implementation

I'm happy to do this. I should be able to knock it out quickly, and I have a Mac to test on.

items.body:
## Purpose and Motivation

This PR adds the possibility of building SuperCollider as a [Linux appimage](https://appimage.org/) (via LINUX_APPIMAGE cmake option), a selfcontained file with all the needed libraries and resources, similar to a macos bundle. This enables:

- Building SuperCollider as an appimage with the CI and make it available for download on S3 or github releases. Any linux distribution with a recent enough kernel, libc and fuse installed should be able to run the executable.
- Run SuperCollider in "portable" mode by having a SuperCollider.AppImage.home folder next to the executable. This implements the historical "standalone" feature of SC. In this mode the binary will not look at anything in the home directory of the user, allowing for self-contained and distributable works.

The appimage can already be tested by downloading from the [artifacts section](https://github.com/supercollider/supercollider/suites/9945865297/artifacts/481656901).

Some notes:
- Because we just remap the HOME folder completely to SuperCollider.AppImage.home there is no need to use or implement "standalone" modes in scide or sclang. Users should put their code inside SuperCollider.AppImage.home
- I have not used the work done in the [Standalone PR for macos bundles](https://github.com/supercollider/supercollider/pull/5898) since the approach here is a bit different. labels.name: bug
labels.description: Issues that relate to unexpected/unwanted behavior. Don't use for PRs.

labels.name: comp: sclang
labels.description: sclang C++ implementation (primitives, etc.). for changes to class lib use "comp: class library"

items.body:
By default, a child process created with `fork` inherits all open file descriptors (including all open sockets), except for those that have the `FD_CLOEXEC` flag set. sclang and scsynth should really set the `FD_CLOEXEC` on all sockets that are bound to a specific port number, otherwise a lingering child process might occupy certain ports, such as the lang port or scsynth port.

Usually, this is not a problem, but some UGens (e.g. `VSTPlugin`) may internally create child processes. This is particularly bad if the child processes becomes a deamon or zombie process because it may block ports indefinitely. (This once happened to me with a VST plugin on a macOS.)

items.title: Misaligned pointers with bump allocators in Scsynth and Supernova

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Issues that relate to unexpected/unwanted behavior. Don't use for PRs.

items.body:
Scsynth and Supernova create Graphs by allocating a single continuous block of memory which is then effectively used as a bump allocator. See https://github.com/supercollider/supercollider/blob/cea67fcd49eb899366d6f7252c70157c5bc8b18f/server/scsynth/SC_Graph.cpp#L94 resp. https://github.com/supercollider/supercollider/blob/cea67fcd49eb899366d6f7252c70157c5bc8b18f/server/supernova/sc/sc_synth.cpp#L69

However, both simply increment the pointer by the desired size and don't consider aligment. `float` and `int` have a natural alignement of 4 bytes, but all pointer types and structures like `Wire` (which contain pointers) have an alignment of 8 bytes (on 64-bit platforms).

For example, if you allocate 3 `int` followed by a `float *`, the latter will be misaligned: https://github.com/supercollider/supercollider/blob/cea67fcd49eb899366d6f7252c70157c5bc8b18f/server/supernova/sc/sc_synth.cpp#L76

---

Supernova might have similar problems in other places where `linear_allocator` is used.

Actually, `linear_allocator` could be improved to take alignment into account. A similiar helper class could be used for scsynth.

items.title: [linux] SystemClock is not reliable shortly after waking from sleep

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Issues that relate to unexpected/unwanted behavior. Don't use for PRs.

labels.name: comp: sclang
labels.description: sclang C++ implementation (primitives, etc.). for changes to class lib use "comp: class library"

items.body:
## Short summary

sclang and scsynth follow `std::chrono::high_resolution_clock`.

- sclang: `schedInit()` (https://github.com/supercollider/supercollider/blob/develop/lang/LangPrimSource/PyrSched.cpp#L240) and `elapsedTime()` (L258-261).

- scsynth: `syncOSCOffsetWithTimeOfDay()` and `resyncThreadFunc()`(https://github.com/supercollider/supercollider/blob/develop/server/scsynth/SC_CoreAudio.cpp#L76-L128)

In Linux, it appears that the high-resolution clock is, in fact, not monotonic. I've observed time jumps of several hundred milliseconds in an instant, when using SC shortly after waking my system from sleep.

Nobody noticed this in some 15+ years of the Linux version existing, probably because there have never been any serious efforts to sync SC with other software. Now we have `LinkClock`, so the problem becomes more visible.

## Environment

* SuperCollider version: 3.10.2
* Operating system: Ubuntu Studio 18.04

## Steps to reproduce

I can reproduce a discontinuity in `SystemClock` times *fairly* reliably this way. There is not a specific amount of time until the problem happens. It may be a couple of minutes, it may be 15-30 minutes.

1. The OS session is suspended. sclang should not be running at the time of putting the computer to sleep.

2. Wake the computer from sleep.

3. Launch SC.

4. Start running some patterns. Eventually there will be a brief period of "late" messages from scsynth. In my experience, it recovers quickly.

Alternately, use a 3.11 test build and run a `LinkClock` alongside an external, non-SC Link peer.

```
TempoClock.default = t = LinkClock.new.latency_(0.2);
// run some patterns
```

When the problem happens, the SC `LinkClock` will desynchronize from the other peers. I've personally witnessed this behavior (SC LinkClock vs Ableton Live). The only way to recover is to reboot the interpreter (reinitializing the SC clocks).

## Expected vs. actual behavior

Expected: 1 second = 1 second, always, within accepted tolerance.

Actual: I have testing data from my DDWOscSyncClocks, where:

Index | Local SystemClock.seconds | Remote SystemClock.seconds | local - remote
------|---------------------------|----------------------------|---------------
1 | 467.835693893 | 531.06219482422 | -63.22650093122
2 | 468.5567713 | 531.17431640625 | -62.61754510625

The remote clock advanced by c. 0.112 sec, and in the same amount of time, the local clock advanced by c. 0.721: over 600 ms ahead of where it should be. Allowing for clocks on different machines to drift slightly over time, it's pretty safe to say that a 500-600% jump ahead is neither within any reasonable tolerance, nor musically useful. Times remained consistent after the jump; clock times were permanently affected.

I'm not sure of all of the ramifications of switching SC in Linux to use a monotonic clock. But this finding is pretty bad. It may be worth some risk.

Windows, btw, is very likely using `QueryPerformanceCounter` which (I think) is monotonic. MacOS, I don't know. It's probably a Linux-only problem.

(Logging for sclang + scsynth + supernova, because their clocks must all agree.)

items.title: Enhancement: `/fail` messages for synchronous commands
items.body:
The Server Command Reference says:

> /fail
> An error occurred.
> 
> string	the name of the command
> string	the error message.
> other	(optional) some commands provide other information, for example a buffer index.
> 
> There was a problem. Sent only to the sender of the original message.

It does not specify that this should be only for asynchronous commands. However, it appears that informally this has been interpreted to apply only to asynchronous commands.

But, if (for example, as happened to me just today) incoming commands are accidentally evaluated out of order such that `/b_setn` precedes `/b_alloc`, certainly the user should get some feedback and I see no reason why this should not include an OSC reply.

`/b_setn` is an especially egregious case because it looks like scsynth doesn't even provide an error post at all!

```
Server.scsynth;
s.boot;

s.sendMsg(\b_setn, 0, 0, 3, 1, 2, 3);
```

Supernova tries to print a message, but a/ this does not include the buffer number and b/ currently there is a typo (#3897) that causes the message posting to be delayed, complicating troubleshooting.

In other words, neither server reports the error properly, and there is no OSC failsafe. Also, without OSC reporting, user code has absolutely no way to detect failure.

We could argue about which commands may not require a reply. I think certainly buffer commands should do it, as they are lower density than for example `/c_set` might be.

Because the documentation is unclear about the spec, I won't say it's a bug (and, accordingly, not for consideration in 3.10).

Proper 64 bit file support for Buffers
items.body:
PA Tremblay queried me off-list about buffers and whether the max number of samples was limited by a 32 bit int. I noted that in bufAlloc, samples is calculated like so:

```long numSamples = numFrames * numChannels;```

but is then stored in the SndBuf as an int. This seemed like an easy fix, and I started a branch, but it raises a couple of issues maybe worth discussing. I think there are three ways this could be dealt with (for all three would make sense to correspondingly change relevant UGen code).

1. Change sample count to be 64 bit. This would allow larger file sizes.
2. Do 1 and change frames to 64 bit. CAF has 64 bit signed frame count. (Also channel count but libsndfile uses an int for channels, so I'm not sure what the point is until that changes. Superlarge channel counts would be exotic to say the least...)
3. Do 1 and 2 and add or convert to a 64 bit int type in sclang and implement support in OSC. Without this certain things would still not work due to the 32 bit limit on communication.

Obviously these are incremental. 3 is the most invasive, and more work than I'm happy to take on at the moment. Is 1 or 2 worth doing now as a step towards that? I don't think it would break anything new.

items.title: No way to see value of control mapped to a bus
Supernova does not implement /error correctly
items.body:
See http://doc.sccode.org/Reference/Server-Command-Reference.html#/error

In supernova, neither use of /error actually prevents error posting.

```supercollider
s.sendBundle(nil,
    #[error, 0],
    Group.basicNew(s, 200).freeMsg,
    #[error, 1]
);

s.sendBundle(nil,
    #[error, -1],
    Group.basicNew(s, 200).freeMsg,
    #[error, -2]
);
```

The use case for /error was thoroughly discussed before it was implemented in scsynth several years ago. It's especially useful for freeing/releasing nodes. If you free a node that exists, the end result is that the node is gone. If you free a node that already disappeared, the end result is the same: the node is gone. But the result in the interface is different: in the latter case, there is an error posting even though the actual situation might not have been an error to begin with.

One could argue that the client should know whether the node is gone or not, but, the client doesn't receive this information synchronously. There are plenty of cases (Voicer, for instance) where the out of date node status in the client does cause spurious "node not found" postings. In turn, this freaks out performers, when they see messages that looks like something went wrong.

Not especially urgent, but it does matter quite a bit to me. The lack of a working /error command wouldn't stop me from using supernova for my own performances, but I would not use it (in this state) for a piece where the performer is looking at the screen during rehearsals or concerts.

items.title: Add a way to map multichannel buses using argument-string syntax

labels.name: comp: sclang
labels.description: sclang C++ implementation (primitives, etc.). for changes to class lib use "comp: class library"

items.body:
Currently there are two ways to map single-channel buses onto SynthDef arguments:
- OSC message (/n_map, /n_mapn)
- Argument syntax: `"argname", "c/n/"` where /n/ is the bus number

But there is only one way to map a multichannel bus onto an array argument:
- /n_mapn

I propose extending argument syntax: `c/n/_/c/` where /c/ is the number of channels to map, e.g. `\freqs, \c0_4` to map four consecutive control buses onto four consecutive inputs. If not given, 1 would be assumed (current behavior).

The change on the language side would be trivial. It would also require a change in the server to handle the number of channels. I believe this wouldn't be especially hard but I don't know the server code very well.

Possible drawback: Currently, you can accidentally map a multichannel bus onto a non-array control, and the additional bus channels do not spill over onto the following controls. That would change. But I think it's reasonable that the user should be responsible for managing the number of bus channels properly.
